summary: Discovery focused on cost per token tradeoffs across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private; Norcross emphasized strict budget cap, regional data residency, SSO/KMS needs, and a 6-8 week pilot timeline. Discussed batching, KV/prefix caching, and fallbacks for latency-sensitive endpoints.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Eli Chen (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (Norcross CTO), James O'Neal (Head of MLOps), Priya Desai (Eng Manager)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — we have Maya and Eli from Redwood, and from Norcross Sofia, James, Priya. Quick agenda: understand your workload and budget constraints, show where levers live (batching, cache, hosting), and agree pilot next steps. Sound good?

[00:18] Sofia (Norcross CTO): Yep that's perfect. We're short on time so we want to get to costs and guardrails. We've been evaluating hosted vendors and also thinking about a private option because of residency and compliance.

[00:28] James (Head of MLOps): To add — our main use case is document ingestion + Q&A across internal knowledge base and customer-facing support chat. Peak concurrency is around 600 qps for short prompts, but avg token lengths vary a lot, 60-300 tokens. Budget-wise the CFO gave us a hard cap of $75k/month for inference initially.

[00:45] Eli (Redwood SE): Okay that's helpful. Do you currently have a way you measure tokens today or is it estimate-based?

[00:51] Priya (Eng Manager): We instrumented a week in December; numbers are a bit noisy — we have an average of 18M tokens/day now but that includes background embeddings jobs. For the chat surface alone it's 6-8M tokens/day.

[01:05] Maya: Great — so 6-8M tokens/day for the customer chat path is our starting point. Two immediate levers you'll see: batching/continuous batching for throughput amortization, and prefix/KV caching for repeated context. We also want to map those levers to Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private choices.

[01:28] Sofia: Walk us through the economics. Hosted vendor proposals we've seen are per-token with a black-box multiplier for context length. We're trying to understand where the biggest wins are.

[01:39] Eli: Sure. High level — per-token price is the baseline. Then levers: batching increases GPU utilization so effective per-token cost falls for high concurrency; KV cache/prefix cache saves decoder tokens for repeated prompts (eg. system prompt or large instruction templates); and model-sizing/quantization picks also change cost. Hosted is easiest to start but less flexible on custom quantization and sometimes residency; Dedicated gives predictable throughput and reserved capacity economics; Private gives you full control for residency/compliance but increases ops and upfront cost.

[02:12] James: We need predictable burn. CFO doesn't like the variable nature of per-token spikes. What does Redwood do for smoothing or capping spend?

[02:22] Maya: We offer quotas and per-route rate limits, cost alerts, and dedicated pools so spikes are absorbed by reserved capacity rather than socket-ing you with huge bills. Also fallback routing to smaller models during bursts can maintain availability while lowering cost.

[02:38] Sofia: Can you give a concrete example? Say 8M tokens/day chat, 65 average tokens/response, peak concurrency 600 qps — what's the delta between Hosted and Dedicated?

[02:49] Eli: Quick back-of-envelope — hosted per-token for a mid-size chat model might be $0.000024 per token for the base model we typically show in our pricing sheet; with continuous batching on a dedicated pool you can get effective token costs down 25-40% depending on TTL/latency tradeoffs. So that $0.000024 could feel like $0.000015–0.000018 for heavy-batch workloads. For 8M tokens/day at $0.000024 that's about $192/day or ~$5.8k/month; with batching discounts you'd be in the $3.9k–4.8k/month range for the chat path. But remember background embeddings and other workloads are separate.

[03:37] Priya: Those numbers look low compared to vendor quotes we've seen. Are we missing something? Embeddings are expensive for us, and also long-context retrievals blow up token counts.

[03:46] Eli: Right — embeddings and long-context retrievals are different levers. Embeddings have different per-unit pricing. For retrieval-augmented generation, we recommend front-loading dense retrieval to limit context length and use prefix caching for frequent templates so you don't re-send the same 2k-token context every time.

[04:07] James: On the residency and KMS front — we must keep customer PII in-region, SSO via SAML mandatory, and keys must be customer-controlled. Does Redwood support that in Hosted?

[04:18] Maya: Hosted supports regionalized retention and private key control via integrated KMS for enterprise accounts, but full customer-managed HSM is part of the Private deployment offering. For SAML/SSO we do SSO for hosted and Dedicated; Private gives you the control plane on your VPC. We can share our SOC2 and ISO docs.

[04:40] Sofia: Good, please send those. Back to cost — the CFO wants a pilot where spending is capped. How do we set that up?

[04:50] Eli: We can do a pilot on Dedicated with a monthly committed spend plus a cap for overages. Alternatively, hosted with per-route quotas and enforced spend caps is possible for initial eval. Dedicated gives you guaranteed throughput SLOs which helps with predictable latency too.

[05:05] Priya: If we go Dedicated for a pilot, what are typical lead times and what about autoscaling for diurnal load?

[05:13] Eli: Lead times for Dedicated capacity are normally 2–4 weeks depending on region. Autoscaling policies can be configured for burst capacity; we also have an 'elastic buffer' for short spikes. For pilot scope we usually provision a pool sized for 50–70% of expected peak and enable burst for short periods, that keeps committed cost down while meeting most spikes.

[05:35] Speaker 1 (transcription hiccup): ...

[05:40] James: One question on batching: if we batch aggressively what impact on latency? We have a 150–200ms 95th percentile SLA on chat messages for premium customers.

[05:49] Eli: Continuous batching is workload-aware — it collects requests for a short window (usually single-digit ms) and runs them together; for high qps that doesn't add much latency. The real tradeoff is when you deliberately hold requests to build larger batches — that increases tail latency. With our routing you can split routes: premium route no batching, or small-window batching; bulk route can be optimized for cost with larger batch windows.

[06:18] Sofia: Ok that split approach sounds promising. Another lever is prefix cache — if the instruction and retrieval tokens are mostly identical, what's the practical cache hit rate you see?

[06:27] Eli: Many customers see 40–70% effective KV/prefix cache hit rates on deterministic system prompts and repeated contexts. That can reduce decoder tokens by the same magnitude for those hits. Important nuance — cache works best when prompts are normalized and retrievals deduplicated.

[06:44] Priya: We're also running LLM-based reranking for search, which is heavy on tokens. Would that be kept on Dedicated or moved to a private cluster?

[06:52] Eli: Reranking at scale often benefits from Dedicated — predictable GPU throughput and lower effective cost per token. If Norcross needs strict data residency for logs and models, Private might be the long-term plan, but Dedicated is commonly how customers start because it balances ops complexity and economics.

[07:12] James: For the pilot we want to surface worst-case monthly burn and a sweet spot for cost/latency. Can you prepare both hosted and dedicated scenarios with numbers?

[07:21] Maya: Yes — we'll provide an itemized comparison: hosted pro forma burn with quotas, dedicated committed + burst pricing, and a private TCO outline. We'll include per-route recommendations.

[07:30] Sofia: We also need to know how the platform exposes token breakdowns so our finance team can map to billing.

[07:36] Eli: Console has per-token and per-route breakdowns at token granularity with export CSVs. We also expose sampling of requests with KV cache hit/miss flags so you can correlate cost to patterns.

[07:49] Priya: That export will be helpful to show the CFO. Any rate for long-context models vs trimmed models? Is there a separate premium?

[07:57] Eli: We price per token regardless of context length, but long-context models tend to have higher per-token execution cost because of increased compute and memory pressure; that shows up in our performance profiles and sometimes in a premium model-based multiplier. We'll point to model profiles in the deck.

[08:15] Sofia: On security, we need audit logs and access controls for engineers. Are RBAC and fine-grained audit logs included?

[08:23] Maya: Yes — role-based access control, session logs, and audit trail are part of Dedicated and Private. Hosted enterprise customers can enable longer audit retention and granular RBAC as an add-on.

[08:35] James: About latency fallbacks — you mentioned routing to smaller models. How automated is that?

[08:41] Eli: We have routing policies you can attach to routes — conditions like CPU/GPU saturation, latency SLO breach, or cost threshold trigger fallbacks. These are configurable in the console and can be automated or manual.

[08:57] Priya: Let's talk concrete pilot sizing. We'll run a 6-week pilot for chat and reranking. We need a committed band that keeps monthly cost under $75k including embeddings. What assumptions do you need from us?

[09:08] Eli: We'll need: daily token profile broken out by route (chat, rerank, embeddings), peak qps per route, average prompt/response token lengths per route, data residency and KMS requirements, and a target latency SLO per route. That lets us simulate burn and recommend hosted vs dedicated split.

[09:25] Sofia: We'll provide that by EOD Wednesday. Also our compliance team will want SOC2 docs and a network diagram for the Private option.

[09:34] Maya: We'll attach the SOC2 and a sample private deployment diagram in the follow-up.

[09:40] Speaker 2 (transcription error): um

[09:44] James: Another question — quantization. Some vendors offer 4-bit quantized models for cheaper inference. Does Redwood support custom quantized models in Dedicated or Private?

[09:54] Eli: Yes. Dedicated supports our verified quantization profiles and we can onboard customer-trained quantized variants on Private. There are model-quality tradeoffs, so we usually run regression tests against your eval set. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization settings per workload.

[10:11] Priya: Regression testing is critical. We'll need to baseline on NDCG for reranking and response quality for chat.

[10:18] Eli: Agreed — we'll propose an eval plan as part of the pilot: baseline sample set, quality thresholds, and automatic regression alerts.

[10:27] Sofia: What about burst pricing? If we commit to X and exceed by Y, are overages billed at a premium?

[10:33] Maya: Overages are billed at an overage rate; delta depends on contract structure. For pilots we often structure a modest overage multiplier to disincentivize unlimited spikes, but also allow short bursts to keep service up. We'll outline a few options.

[10:47] James: On instrumentation — can we hook into tracing to debug tail latency and tokenization issues?

[10:53] Eli: Yes — the platform integrates with distributed tracing and exports request-level timing including batch queuing time, kernel time estimates, and decode time. That helps you pinpoint where latency accumulates.

[11:05] Priya: Nice. Another operational question: how do you handle KV cache invalidation if our retrieval index refreshes frequently?

[11:12] Eli: Cache invalidation policies can be TTL-based, or you can trigger programmatic invalidation for specific keys via API. For frequently changing retrievals we recommend short TTLs and relying on fast retrieval to keep context small.

[11:25] Sofia: For the pilot, we want a price projection for the worst month — assume 12M tokens/day combined across workloads. Can you provide a conservative hosted and dedicated estimate?

[11:34] Eli: We'll produce three scenarios: conservative (no caching, minimal batching), expected (some caching, moderate batching), and optimistic (high cache hit and batching). That should cover worst and best cases.

[11:45] Maya: We'll include explicit line items for embeddings, reranking, and chat. Also call out where configuration changes would materially reduce burn (e.g., dedupe retrievals, normalize prompts).

[11:58] James: Perfect. Any legal or procurement timing we should be aware of? They normally take 2–3 weeks for a pilot contract.

[12:06] Sofia: And procurement will want SLAs for Dedicated pilot.

[12:10] Maya: We'll draft a pilot MOU with SLAs for availability and latency, and include a short appendix on data residency and KMS controls.

[12:20] Priya: One last quick question — do you support hybrid routing where we keep PII queries on Private and the rest on Hosted?

[12:28] Eli: Yes — smart routing by policy is a core feature. You can route by metadata fields, user classes, or content-based tagging to different deployment targets.

[12:40] Sofia: Great. Thanks — this was helpful.

[12:45] Maya: Recap / next steps: we'll send the pricing grid and pilot MOU, Eli will run the traffic sim and provide burn projections, and Norcross will send token profile + compliance checklist. We'll aim to reconvene after you review the docs and run the benchmark.

[12:58] James: Thanks, everyone. Look forward to the numbers.

[13:02] End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional speaker mislabeling and small transcription errors. Natural speech patterns preserved, with interruptions and clarifications.
